title: Keep the night's rebalancing from hanging

blocks.text: A warehouse service moves stock between storage bins: pickers move units to the packing bins all day, and a rebalancing job moves them back at night. Auditors count pairs of bins while both run. Each bin's quantity is guarded by the bin's own monitor, and an operation on two bins holds both, so that nobody ever sees units that are in neither bin. Some nights the rebalancing job stops making progress, and the morning's thread dump shows threads that each hold one bin.

Finish `move(...)` and `count(...)` in `src/main/java/practice/Warehouse.java`. Both are written except for the call that holds the two bins: `holdingBoth(first, second, action)` takes `first`'s monitor, then `second`'s, and runs `action`. Moves in any direction and counts of any pair must be able to run at the same time without ever hanging. About four lines in total.
The tests line two operations up: once one holds its first bin, it lets the other one catch up before taking the second.

cases.says: a move updates both bins, and a move larger than the source bin holds changes nothing
counting two bins gives their total, in either argument order
two moves between the same two bins in opposite directions, at the same time, both finish
a count of two bins that runs at the same time as a move between them finishes, and so does the move

origin.section: Two Locks Taken in Opposite Orders Deadlock; One Order for Every Pair Prevents It

concepts: Two locks taken in opposite orders deadlock; one fixed, unique order used by every piece of code that takes two of the locks prevents it.
